title: Why do Latinos work for ICE?
excerpt: Half of border agents are Latino, and they are part of a long history of Hispanic support for – and enforcement of – harsh immigration policies
content_html:
Since Trump’s return to power, more than 60 people have died at the hands of or in the custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), including two Latino immigrants in one week: Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine. Many Latinos have come to feel that their brown skin makes them targets, and they are not wrong.

But there is another dimension of this story that we often fail to consider: many of those in charge of anti-immigrant operations also have brown skin, Hispanic names and links to the communities they terrorize. When the identities of the agents who killed Alex Pretti in January were revealed as those of two Hispanic men, many people reacted with shock. The irony seemed obvious, but it reflected a mistaken assumption: that Latinos are naturally opposed to restrictionist immigration policies. History suggests otherwise.

Latinos have been not only frequent targets of nativism and xenophobic violence but also supporters – regularly enforcers – of it. For decades, Latinos have joined the border patrol (and since it was established in 2003, ICE) in significant numbers. Latinos now make up a majority of border patrol officers and constitute about 20-30% of ICE agents. More broadly, Latino voters have often supported harsh policies and politicians that would tighten US borders and target immigrant families and communities. Reactionary politics in the United States are not simply imposed on Latinos; they have repeatedly found traction within Latino communities themselves.

Why? Latinos have often occupied an uneasy middle ground in American society – subject to discrimination and exclusion, yet also susceptible to appeals that promise belonging, security and status. Like every other group, they can embrace political movements that harm others and sometimes even themselves.

This precarity is why Latinos join immigration enforcement agencies in such large numbers. For years, scholars and historians have tried to find other explanations, including economics and stable employment, a desire to serve their communities and seeking proximity to whiteness. But these capture only part of the story.

The phenomenon began as early as the 1950s, when prominent Latino leaders and organizations supported deportation campaigns such as Operation Wetback, which sought to remove hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants (and their citizen family members) from the country. Their support was often rooted in not entirely unfounded fears of labor competition; US employers routinely used migrant labor to undermine unions, suppress wages and break strikes.

This logic persisted into the 1960s and 1970s. The United Farm Workers union frequently treated undocumented workers as threats to labor organizing. Union activists routinely harassed migrants, reported them to immigration authorities and even organized their own patrols along the border, some of which resulted in violence against immigrants.

Yet attitudes were always in flux. The civil rights movement transformed US racial politics. The rise of Black Power influenced Chicano activism, and many Mexican Americans increasingly shed illusions that they could be seen as white, at least legally so, and rejected assimilationist impulses. Support for restrictionist policies did not disappear, but it became less dominant in many Latino political circles.

Nevertheless, nativist undercurrents never vanished. Concerns about labor competition remained, as did anxieties about belonging, status and what new waves of immigration might mean for Latinos’ own place in American society. Latinos were ambivalent about Proposition 187, the 1994 California ballot initiative that sought to deny immigrants and their families access to social services. Although only a quarter of them supported the proposition in the end, polling suggested that nearly half considered voting in favor of it in the months and weeks leading up to the vote.

“Latinos for Trump” factions contributed significantly to the rise of Donald Trump and his Maga movement in 2016. And when he ran for re-election in 2024, he did not merely retain significant Latino support; he expanded it. His gains were especially notable among Latino men and in heavily Latino border regions. Counties along the US-Mexico border, including some with large or even majority-Latino populations, shifted toward Trump.

Meanwhile, the American right was increasingly united less by biological notions of race and more by opposition to multiculturalism, feminism, LGBTQ+ rights, immigration and liberalism. Race still mattered, but the boundaries of political belonging became more flexible and expansive.

The right increasingly included prominent figures of color, from Thomas Sowell and Clarence Thomas to Linda Chavez and Marco Rubio. More recently, even parts of the fringe far right have embraced Latino leaders and activists who share their political commitments. Consider figures such as the January 6 insurrectionist (and recipient of a Trump pardon) Enrique Tarrio, leader of the self-described “western chauvinist” Proud Boys, who is Afro-Cuban, or Nick Fuentes, the white supremacist influencer whose father is Mexican American.

That evolution helps explain why some Latinos have found these movements appealing. They offer inclusion on specific terms. They allow participants – immigration agents included – to see themselves not as victims or outsiders, but as defenders of order, tradition and (admittedly vague, sometimes violent notions of) American values.

The lesson here is not that Latinos are uniquely reactionary. Far from it. Every community contains contradictions. Every group produces both opponents and defenders of the status quo. And recent polls suggest that Latinos have begun to swing away from Trump and the Republicans.

The lesson is that we should stop treating Latino support for anti-immigration politics as a paradox. To the contrary, this is a part of a long history, a much longer story. Understanding that history does not require exclusion. But it does require acknowledging it.

  • Eladio Bobadilla is a historian at the University of Pittsburgh and author of Dangerous Migration: Mexican Labor and the Fight for Immigrant Rights. This was written for Zócalo Public Square and republished with its permission

content_html_zh:
自特朗普重新掌权以来，已有 60 多人死于移民和海关执法局 (ICE) 之手或拘留期间，其中包括一周内两名拉丁裔移民：休斯顿的洛伦佐·萨尔加多·阿劳霍和缅因州的琼·塞巴斯蒂安·杜兰·格雷罗。 许多拉丁裔人开始觉得他们的棕色皮肤使他们成为目标，他们没有错。

但这个故事还有另一个我们经常忽略的方面：许多负责反移民行动的人也有棕色皮肤、西班牙裔名字以及与他们所恐吓的社区的联系。 当一月份杀害亚历克斯·普雷蒂的特工身份被揭露为两名西班牙裔男子时，许多人都感到震惊。 讽刺似乎很明显，但它反映了一个错误的假设：拉丁裔天生反对限制主义移民政策。 历史表明事实并非如此。

拉丁裔不仅经常成为本土主义和仇外暴力的目标，而且也是这些行为的支持者——经常的执行者。 几十年来，大量拉丁裔加入了边境巡逻队（自 2003 年成立以来，即加入了 ICE）。 目前，拉丁裔占边境巡逻人员的大多数，并约占 ICE 特工的 20-30%。 更广泛地说，拉丁裔选民往往支持严厉的政策和政客，这些政策和政客会收紧美国边境并针对移民家庭和社区。 美国的反动政治不只是强加给拉丁裔，而是强加给拉丁裔。他们一再在拉丁裔社区中找到了吸引力。

为什么？ 拉丁裔在美国社会中常常处于不稳定的中间地带——受到歧视和排斥，但也容易受到承诺归属感、安全感和地位的吸引力。 与其他群体一样，他们可能会拥抱伤害他人、有时甚至伤害自己的政治运动。

这种不稳定是拉丁裔如此大量加入移民执法机构的原因。 多年来，学者和历史学家一直试图寻找其他解释，包括经济和稳定就业、服务社区的愿望以及寻求接近白人。 但这些只是故事的一部分。

这种现象早在 20 世纪 50 年代就开始了，当时著名的拉丁裔领导人和组织支持“湿背行动”等驱逐运动，该行动旨在将数十万无证移民（及其公民家庭成员）驱逐出该国。 他们的支持往往源于对劳动力竞争的担忧，这并非完全没有根据。美国雇主经常利用移民劳工来破坏工会、压低工资和破坏罢工。

这种逻辑一直持续到 20 世纪 60 年代和 1970 年代。 联合农场工人工会经常将无证工人视为对劳工组织的威胁。 工会活动分子经常骚扰移民，向移民当局举报，甚至组织自己的边境巡逻，其中一些导致针对移民的暴力行为。

然而态度总是在变化。 民权运动改变了美国的种族政治。 黑人权力的崛起影响了奇卡诺的激进主义，许多墨西哥裔美国人越来越多地放弃了自己可以被视为白人的幻想，至少在法律上是这样，并拒绝同化主义冲动。 对限制主义政策的支持并未消失，但在许多拉丁裔政界中的主导地位有所减弱。

然而，本土主义的暗流从未消失。 对劳动力竞争的担忧依然存在，对归属感、地位以及新一波移民浪潮可能对拉丁裔在美国社会中的地位意味着什么的焦虑也依然存在。 拉丁美洲人对 187 号提案持矛盾态度，该提案是 1994 年加州投票倡议，旨在剥夺移民及其家人获得社会服务的机会。 尽管最终只有四分之一的人支持这一提议，但民意调查显示，近一半的人在投票前的几个月和几周内考虑投票赞成。

“拉丁美洲人支持特朗普”派别对唐纳德·特朗普及其 2016 年马加运动的崛起做出了重大贡献。 当他在 2024 年竞选连任时，他不仅保留了拉丁裔的大量支持，而且还获得了巨大的支持。他扩展了它。 他的进步在拉丁裔男性和拉丁裔人口密集的边境地区尤其显着。 美墨边境沿线的县，包括一些人口众多甚至以拉丁裔为主的县，都转向了特朗普。

与此同时，美国右翼越来越多地通过反对多元文化主义、女权主义、LGBTQ+权利、移民和自由主义而团结起来，而不是种族的生物学概念。 种族仍然很重要，但政治归属的界限变得更加灵活和广泛。

右翼越来越多地包括著名的有色人种人物，从托马斯·索威尔和克拉伦斯·托马斯到琳达·查韦斯和马可·卢比奥。 最近，甚至部分极右翼边缘人士也拥抱了有着共同政治承诺的拉丁裔领导人和活动人士。 想想1月6日的叛乱分子（也是特朗普赦免的获得者）恩里克·塔里奥（Enrique Tarrio），他是自称“西方沙文主义”的“骄傲男孩”（Proud Boys）的领导人，他是非裔古巴人；或者尼克·富恩特斯（Nick Fuentes），一位父亲是墨西哥裔美国人的白人至上主义影响者。

这种演变有助于解释为什么一些拉丁美洲人发现这些运动很有吸引力。 他们提供特定条款的包容性。 它们让参与者——包括移民代理——不把自己视为受害者或局外人，而是秩序、传统和（诚然是模糊的，有时是暴力的概念）美国价值观的捍卫者。

这里的教训并不是拉丁裔是独一无二的反动分子。 远非如此。 每个社会都存在着矛盾。 每个群体都会产生现状的反对者和捍卫者。 最近的民意调查显示，拉丁裔已经开始远离特朗普和共和党。

教训是，我们不应再将拉丁裔对反移民政治的支持视为一个悖论。 相反，这是一个悠久历史的一部分，一个更长的故事。 了解历史并不需要排除。 但它确实需要承认这一点。

  • 埃拉迪奥·博巴迪拉（Eladio Bobadilla）是匹兹堡大学的历史学家，也是《危险移民：墨西哥劳工与移民权利之战》一书的作者。 本文是为索卡洛公共广场撰写的，并经其许可重新发布
